For carcinoma of the stomach, surgery is the primary therapy, but is possible in only approximately 50% of patients at diagnosis. A
In locoregional advanced disease, the addition of postoperative chemoradiation therapy or preoperative chemotherapy has been shown to improve survival. A

background.definition: Carcinoma of the stomach is a relatively uncommon malignancy in the United States but has a much higher prevalence in other nations. At diagnosis, most cases of gastric cancer are at least locally advanced because of its vague presentation.

list.listitem: In the United States approximately 22,000 new cases and 11,500 deaths per year.

There are large geographic variations in incidence: highest in most of Asia, areas of South America, and Eastern Europe. Incidence is lowest in North America, much of Africa, Southeast Asia, and Northern Europe.
Mean age at diagnosis is 65 years; more common in men than women (1.5:1).

In one population-based study of 250,000 British patients, there were 319 cases of gastric cancer in 7 years, of which 25 occurred in persons younger than 55 years, and only 1 of whom had no alarm symptoms.
Multifactorial: see table of risk factors for gastric cancer.

Helicobacter pylori is an important risk factor, and a systematic review concluded that eradication of HP reduces the subsequent risk of gastric cancer (pooled incidence rate ratio 0.53, 95% CI, 0.44-0.64).
A global consensus statement on promoting HP eradication to prevent gastric cancer has been developed, although further work is required to confirm the best strategy for screening populations.
An intervention study in a Hispanic population in Colombia confirmed the efficacy of H pylori therapy in reducing progression of metaplasia to gastric cancer over a 20 year follow-up period.
A systematic review and meta-analysis addressing consumption of ultraprocessed food (UPF) showed a correlation between the highest UPF group and risk of non-cardia gastric cancer.

The Lauren classification system describes two distinct types of gastric cancer. The intestinal type is more common in males and older patients, is located predominantly in the distal stomach and antrum, and has a better prognosis. The diffuse/infiltrative type is more common in younger patients, is located predominantly in the proximal stomach and GE junction, and has a worse prognosis.

For intestinal type, risk factors such as Helicobacter pylori pernicious anemia and a high-salt diet may incite a progression of changes from chronic superficial gastritis to atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, and finally adenocarcinoma.

For diffuse type, the pathogenesis is less clear, but the loss of expression of E-cadherin (CDH1), an epithelial cell adhesion protein, has been implicated. Germline CDH1 mutations with a penetrance of 70% have been identified in families with hereditary diffuse gastric cancer.
Adenocarcinoma accounts for 90% to 95% of cases, but other histologies include lymphoma, leiomyosarcoma, carcinoid, squamous cell carcinoma, and gastrointestinal stromal tumors.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Previous gastrectomy: eg, Billroth I or II

list.listitem: In countries with a low incidence of gastric cancer, such as the United States, screening for gastric cancer is not routinely recommended. C

There is no consensus regarding screening in high-risk populations. The higher 5-year survival rate from gastric cancer in Japan (>50%) may be related to screening. However, the data are limited by considerable length and lead-time bias. C
A recent large randomised trial of screening in China identified a significant survival advantage for screening endoscopy in populations within high risk area.

A population review of patients treated between 1990 and 2018 demonstrates increased risk of development of gastric cancer with prescription of proton pump inhibitors compared to H2 receptor antagonists. This review included over 1 million patients in total and attempted to adjust for confounding risk factors. The use of PPI was found to increase risk of gastric cancer with more effect if higher dose and for longer duration which has implications for prescribing recommendation to use H2RA first and minimise PPI prescription. A systematic review of 15 observational studies also found an increase in the risk of gastric cancer (RR 1.67, 95% CI 1.39 - 2.0) but the absolute risk increase is very small.

Detection and eradication of H. pylori is an emerging screening technique in high-risk populations. A systematic review concluded that eradication of HP reduces the subsequent risk of gastric cancer (pooled incidence rate ratio 0.53, 95% CI, 0.44-0.64).B
Antioxidants are not effective in the prevention of gastric cancer. B

A large long-term trial (22.3 years) in a high risk area of China found a reduction in gastric cancer death from intervention with H pylori eradication therapy a vitamin C, vitamin E and selenium supplement (but not from use of garlic).
Presenting symptoms are mostly commonly loss of appetite, weight loss, and abdominal pain of recent onset. Physical examination is useful for detecting signs of advanced disease. C
Definitive diagnosis is typically made by upper endoscopy and biopsy. C
After pathologic confirmation, staging and preoperative evaluation consist of laboratory studies, CT abdomen and pelvis, CXR or CT chest, and possibly PET/CT. C

Suspect gastric cancer in patients with recent onset of dyspepsia who are over age 55 years, and in anyone with alarm symptoms. Positive predictive value for any alarm symptom (weight loss, dysphagia, black stools, blood in stools) is 3% based on a population-based study of 7000 patients presenting with dysphagia and followed for 3 years.
Gastric cancer is exceedingly rare among patients under age 55 years, especially in the absence of alarm symptoms (1 in 100,000 over a 7 year period in one large population-based study in Britain).

The most common initial symptoms are loss of appetite, weight loss, and abdominal pain. The Duration of symptoms is often short (<3 months). Proximal lesions are associated with dysphagia, indigestion, anorexia, and postprandial fullness. Distal lesions are associated with gastric outlet obstruction.

In one large study, approximately a third of patients with dyspepsia and suspected gastric cancer by endoscopy did not present with alarm symptoms (vomiting, weight loss, and evidence of GI blood loss).

Physical examination may indicate signs of advanced disease. Signs of peritoneal carcinomatosis include ascites, Krukenberg’s tumor (enlarged ovary), Blumer’s shelf (rectal mass), and "Sister Mary Joseph’s node" (periumbilical adenopathy). Signs of distant nodal spread include Virchow’s node (left supraclavicular) and Irish node (left axillary).
Overall clinical suspicion by a primary-care physician is very specific but not very sensitive.

Initial study should be upper endoscopy with biopsy, which yields a diagnosis in most patients. The sensitivity of a single biopsy has been reported to be 70%, but is 95% with 4 biopsies at the ulcer margin and base, and is over 98% with 7 biopsies. If not available, an upper GI study is an alternative but is much less sensitive and does not allow tissue sampling.
The initial workup should include CBC with platelets, complete metabolic profile, abdominal CT, CT/ultrasound pelvis for women, and CXR. PET/CT and endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) are optional.

British guidelines recommend initial staging with CT of thorax, abdomen, and pelvis. The utility of CT is primarily in excluding grossly metastatic disease, such as liver or distant nodal involvement. CT is less sensitive for peritoneal seeding. Laparoscopy is recommended for all patients with gastric cancer as part of staging.

EUS allows fine-needle aspiration biopsy of nodes and is superior to CT in assessing depth of tumor invasion and lymph node involvement. In a prospective comparison of CT, EUS, and intraoperative assessment, the accuracy for T-stage was 43%, 86%, and 56% and N-stage was 51%, 74%, and 54%, respectively. However, EUS is more invasive than CT, rarely affects treatment decisions, and is not recommended by the National Comprehensive Care Network (NCCN) as part of initial staging or preoperative evaluation.

PET/CT has greater sensitivity for distant metastasis compared with CT, but this is less so for peritoneal carcinomatosis. Therefore, the NCCN cautions that PET/CT has limited utility if the disease is already confirmed as T1 or M1.
A diagnostic accuracy study in 256 patients, 21 of whom had a synchronous advanced colorectal cancer, F-FDG PET/CT was 76% sensitive and 96% specific.

Staging laparoscopy identifies occult peritoneal or liver metastases in 20% to 30% of cases and should be considered for patients who are otherwise candidates for definitive surgery or neoadjuvant therapy.
Paracentesis with cytology should be performed if ascites is present.
Tumor markers are not recommended because elevated values are not helpful in predicting recurrence.
Current ASCO and American College Pathology guidelines recommend determination of HER2 status in gastric cancer, as this will inform treatment options.
A clinical decision rule to predict the likelihood of recurrence after surgery for gastric cancer has been developed and validated.

Suspect gastric cancer in patients with recent onset of loss of appetite, weight loss, and/or abdominal pain. Endoscopy is also recommended for patients with new dyspepsia presenting after age 55 years.
If gastric cancer is suspected, upper endoscopy is the preferred initial step, with barium studies as an alternative.
If confirmed pathologically, then complete staging and preoperative evaluation should be performed.
Surgery is the primary therapy for gastric cancer. A

For patients with T1N0 disease, operative/limited resection is recommended by ESMO guidelines. Patients with more advanced operable disease should undergo pre-operative chemotherapy, surgery, and post-operative chemotherapy. A
Chemotherapy plus nivolumab for first line therapy of HER2 negative advanced gastric and oesophageal adenocarcinoma significantly improves overall survival compared with chemotherapy alone.B

Further evidence for improved survival with combination of immunotherapy and chemotherapy comes from a Chinese study of 885 patients comparing CAPOX chemotherapy (capecitabine plus oxaliplatin) alone with or without addition of camrelizumab. Overall survival improved with immunotherapy from 12.5 to 15 months.

A small Chinese study randomising patients between neo-adjuvant chemoradiotherapy or not followed by adjuvant chemotherapy post-operatively found that the neo-adjuvant treatment significantly improved the rate of R0 resection and subsequent progression free survival. B
For patients with inoperable or metastatic disease choosing therapy, chemotherapy is recommended. A
Surgery remains the primary therapy for locoregional disease when possible.

European Society of Medical Oncology recommend the following: Operable Stage T1N0 disease: consider endoscopic/limited resection Operable Stage > T1N0 disease: pre-operative chemotherapy, followed by surgery and post-operative chemotherapy. Inoperable or metastatic disease: if active treatment sought, begin with palliative chemotherapy. If HER-2 negative, offer platinum + fluoropyrimidine-based doublet or triplet regimen. If HER2 positive offer trastuzumab + cisplatin/5-FU or cisplatin/capecitabine. Also consider clinical trials of novel agents. This may be followed by second-line chemotherapy. Publication of these guidelines dates back to 2016 and the advent of immunotherapy options since then has altered the treatment options- see below.

Endoscopic laser surgery can be considered for T1N0 lesions that are small (≤2 cm), clearly confined to the mucosa, well-differentiated, and non-ulcerated. However, open surgical resection is still considered the standard of care, as RCTs are lacking of endoscopic mucosal resection.

A meta-analysis of 23 trials and 7336 patients demonstrated comparable outcomes between laparoscopic and open gastrectomy, which opens the way for less invasive surgical approaches. A large RCT with 1039 comparing laparoscopic and open gastrectomy found that 3 year disease-free survival was similar between groups.
Newer surgical developments using robotic surgery compare favourably with laparoscopic gastrectomy in terms of recovery time and may improve the extent of lymphadenectomy.

A network meta-analysis of 22 RCTs with 6890 patients compared minimally invasive, open and robotic gastrectomy. Minimally invasive surgery was non-inferior with regards to survival and recurrence, and was associated with less surgical morbidity.
Subtotal gastrectomy is recommended when possible. Long-term outcomes are similar to those of total gastrectomy, assuming that widely negative margins and an adequate lymphadenectomy can be achieved.
Special considerations: Proximal lesions generally require total gastrectomy. T4 lesions require en bloc resection to achieve negative margins. Splenectomy should be avoided if possible.

Several randomized trials have shown no benefit to more extensive lymph node dissection (D1 vs D2). D1 resection includes the tumor and perigastric nodes. D2 resection also includes second echelon nodes and en bloc distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy (for proximal tumors). Any oncologic benefit from a D2 resection may be offset by greater perioperative complications. British Guidelines recommend D2 lymphadenectomy for patients with stage II or III cancer who are fit enough for the procedure. Extended lymphadenectomy may be warranted in patients with N2 disease. Resections that include less than complete dissection of the perigastric nodes (D0) should be avoided.
Use of an anti-adhesive agent intraoperatively (Guardix-SG) found a lower likelihood of bowel adhesions at one year in patients undergoing radical gastrectomy (7.3% vs 20%, NNT = 8).

Randomization between preoperative chemoradiotherapy and perioperative chemotherapy for resectable patients demonstrated no survival advantage for the preoperative chemoradiotherapy group, even though there was higher pathological response rate at surgery.

Adjuvant chemoradiation therapy is recommended for T3-4 and/or node-positive disease. One study reported improved relapse-free and overall survival (50 vs 41% at 3 years, P = .005, NNT = 11) with the addition of 5-FU/leucovorin and radiation therapy compared with surgery alone.

In patients receiving adjuvant chemotherapy post surgical resection, a placebo controlled trial concluded that addition of celecoxib in COX2 positive patients proved effective in improving overall survival as well as progression free survival and quality of life.

Adjuvant chemotherapy without radiation is not thought to improve overall survival. Several phase III trials of 5-FU, adriamycin, and mitomycin C have been negative. Several meta-analyses of adjuvant chemotherapy have yielded conflicting results.
Adjuvant radiation therapy without chemotherapy reduces locoregional failure rate but has not been shown to provide survival benefit.

In 2021 the Checkmate 577 international trial was published in which patients with residual pathology at resection of esophageal or esophageal junction disease were randomised to nivolumab immunotherapy (PD1 inhibitor) or placebo. The median progression free survival in the 532 patients treated with nivolumab was 22.4 months compared to 11 months in the placebo arm.

In the neoadjuvant setting, the MAGIC trial concluded that perioperative epirubicin, cisplatin, and 5-FU improved progression-free and overall survival at 3 years (36 vs 23%, P = .009, NNT = 8) compared with surgery alone.
A small (n = 76) RCT of surgery versus neoadjuvant chemoradiation has shown increased R0 resection in the neoadjuvant group supporting this treatment pathway for operable disease.
Preoperative radiation has been shown to improve complete resection rate, local failure, regional failure, and survival compared with surgery alone.

Definitive combined-modality chemoradiation therapy can be used to treat surgically unresectable or medically inoperable patients. An old series suggested a survival benefit of adding chemotherapy to radiation.
Even in locally advanced patients, significant long-term survival (18%) has been reported with chemoradiation approaches.
Multiagent chemotherapy alone provided a median survival of 14 to 18 months in 2 trials.
A Cochrane review concluded that there was a survival benefit for chemotherapy in patients with advanced disease compared to placebo, increasing survival by about 7 months.

The Checkmate 649 international trial assessed chemotherapy alone versus chemotherapy plus nivolumab for first line therapy of HER2 negative advanced gastric and oesophageal adenocarcinoma. With 1581 patients, this demonstrated significant benefit in overall survival (HR 0.71) and progression free survival for the nivolumab arm. This has been proposed as a new standard of care.

The role of neoadjuvant therapy in improving resectability is being investigated. One phase II trial of neoadjuvant chemoradiation therapy in stage IB-III disease reported favorable rates of R0 resection (77%), pathologic CR (26%), D2 dissection (50%), and median overall survival (23 months).

Patients with metastatic or recurrent disease have a very poor prognosis and should be offered best supportive care, chemotherapy, or enrollment in a clinical trial depending on their performance status.

Meta-analyses of patients with advanced disease have shown that chemotherapy improves survival and quality of life compared with best supportive care alone. A Cochrane review identified 60 RCTs of 11,698 patients and concluded that chemotherapy for patients with advanced gastric cancer increases survival by approximately 7 months. For metastatic disease, common chemotherapeutic regimens include multiagent use of 5-FU, platinum compounds, anthracyclines, irinotecan, taxanes, etoposide, and mitomycin-C. The NCCN gives a category 1 recommendation for taxane-based regimens or ECF.
Immunotherapy has been tested in the advanced disease setting in the KEYNOTE061 trial. Pembrolizumab did not improve overall survival compared to single agent taxol.

Local therapies for best supportive care include endoluminal stents, endoscopic laser, gastrostomy tube, photodynamic therapy, and short courses of radiation therapy. Surgical resection may be appropriate for highly selected patients.
A Cochrane review concluded that corticosteroids may help resolve bowel obstruction in patients with advanced gastric cancer, based on a favorable trend in a small number of studies.
Post-gastrectomy, ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) in a dose of 300 mg to 600 mg once daily reduces the likelihood of gallstone formation (OR 0.20-0.27).
In Western countries, 5 year overall survival is approximately 50% for T3N0, 10% to 30% for N1-2 disease, and <10% for N3-4. A
The addition of postoperative chemoradiation therapy or perioperative chemotherapy has improved survival rates for locoregional advanced disease. A
A validated clinical rule can predict the likelihood of recurrence after surgery for gastric cancer.
Direct extension may occur to the omenta, diaphragm, pancreas, transverse colon, small bowel, spleen, liver, left adrenal gland, left kidney, and superior mesenteric/celiac vessels.
Abundant lymphatics are present within the submucosal and subserosal layers of the stomach.
Hematogenous spread occurs via the portal vein (liver metastases) or systemic circulation (bone and lung metastases).
Peritoneal spread can occur if the gastric wall is penetrated.

Surgery alone yields excellent 5-year overall survival for early stage disease (80%-90%). In Western countries, 5 year survival is approximately 50% for T3N0, 10% to 30% for N1-2 disease, and <10% for N3-4. The Japanese literature reports higher figures. For resected disease, the addition of postoperative chemoradiation or perioperative chemotherapy increases 3-year survival by 9% to 13%.
After surgery alone with curative intent, the locoregional failure rate is reported as 38% as any component of failure. These high rates of failure provide a rationale for postoperative therapies.
A clinical decision rule to predict the likelihood of recurrence after surgery was developed in 536 patients and validated in 122.
After definitive therapy, patients should be followed every 4 to 6 months for 3 years, then annually.
Nutritional care should remain aggressive.
Endoscopy and CT scans should be included in followup, but there is no consensus regarding the surveillance schedule.
